title: Frequency of infraposition and missing contact points in implant‐supported restorations within natural dentitions over time: A systematic review with meta‐analysis

subsections.subsection_title: Biologic and Clinical Foundations of Dental Implant Therapy
subsections.content:
Dental implant therapy is founded on osseointegration, whereby direct structural and functional contact between bone and implant permits stable support for prosthetic reconstruction. Contemporary consensus evidence indicates that implant-supported single crowns and fixed dental prostheses are highly predictable over 5- and 10-year intervals, with implant survival commonly exceeding 95%, establishing implants as a reliable treatment option within natural dentitions when case selection and maintenance are appropriate ref [1].

Yet the biologic basis of osseointegration must be distinguished from long-term restorative success. Consensus and retrospective cohort data show that prosthetic complications remain common despite excellent survival, including screw or abutment loosening, loss of retention, and especially veneering-material fracture or chipping ref [1], ref [2]. In a 10-year retrospective analysis, reconstruction survival reached 95.5%, but overall prosthetic success was lower because nearly one quarter of restorations exhibited mechanical or technical complications, with ceramic chipping the dominant event ref [2].

Clinically, these observations are central to the present review topic because implants behave as ankylosed units lacking periodontal ligament-mediated eruption and adaptive mobility. This biomechanical distinction from natural teeth helps explain both their favorable fixation and their susceptibility to relative positional change against adjacent dentition over time. It also underscores the importance of prosthetic design, occlusal management, peri-implant tissue health, and structured supportive care when interpreting long-term outcomes such as infraposition and open or missing proximal contacts in implant-supported restorations ref [1], ref [2].

subsections.subsection_title: Growth, Eruption, and Implant Placement in Developing Dentitions
subsections.content:
Implant placement in developing dentitions is constrained by a fundamental biologic asymmetry: natural teeth continue erupting and the alveolar process continues remodeling during adolescence and even early adulthood, whereas osseointegrated implants behave functionally like ankylosed units and do not participate in these adaptive movements ref [3], ref [4]. Classic implant-method studies showed substantial post-emergent vertical and sagittal eruption of maxillary incisors and molars from childhood into the third decade, underscoring why implant timing cannot be based on tooth emergence alone ref [3].

Clinical follow-up studies in adolescents confirmed this concern. In late mixed or recently completed permanent dentitions, implant survival may be high, yet infraocclusion of implant crowns can develop when residual craniofacial growth persists, particularly in the anterior maxilla where esthetic discrepancies are most visible ref [4]. In the Gothenburg cohort, vertical discrepancy was linked more closely to skeletal maturation and residual body growth than to chronological age, leading to the recommendation that dental and skeletal maturity—not age alone—should guide treatment planning ref [4].

Longer observation strengthens the same message. In an 8-year follow-up of single implants in the upper incisor region, most restorations remained functional, but gradual infraposition and altered relationships to adjacent teeth were documented, including in some patients treated after adolescence; continued eruption of neighboring teeth and loss of interincisal contact were implicated ref [5]. These findings establish the conceptual basis for the present review: infraposition and missing contact points are time-dependent phenomena arising from persistent dentoalveolar change around a fixed implant restoration, especially in anterior sites placed before complete growth stabilization ref [3], ref [4], ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Regenerative and Adjunctive Approaches Around Implants
subsections.content:
Regenerative and adjunctive procedures around implants are conceptually relevant to infraposition and interproximal contact stability because peri-implant hard- and soft-tissue architecture influences the apparent vertical position of the restoration, papillary fill, and the maintenance of proximal relationships over time. Guided bone regeneration (GBR), simultaneous contour augmentation, and soft-tissue thickening are therefore not merely esthetic refinements, but determinants of how implant-supported crowns integrate within a changing natural dentition. Early controlled evidence showed that synthetic barrier approaches can support peri-implant defect resolution and radiographic bone fill, helping establish a more stable peri-implant foundation for prosthetic emergence ref [6].

The biologic rationale for these adjunctive therapies is well supported by studies on contour augmentation and tissue phenotype modification. Simultaneous GBR with implants placed in esthetic sites has been associated with favorable ridge preservation and contour maintenance, while connective tissue grafting and buccal soft-tissue augmentation improve mucosal thickness and reduce recession risk around single implants. These measures are especially pertinent when small vertical discrepancies later develop, because preserved crestal support and soft-tissue volume may mask minor infraposition and limit the clinical expression of open contact areas by sustaining papillary architecture and emergence profile continuity.

At the same time, regenerative procedures do not eliminate the underlying cause of implant infraposition or proximal contact loss, namely the continued eruption, drift, and remodeling of adjacent natural teeth relative to an ankylosed implant. Thus, adjunctive strategies should be framed as risk-modifying rather than preventive. In growing or borderline young adult patients, they may improve the tolerance of future discrepancies and facilitate later prosthetic correction, but they cannot substitute for careful timing of implant placement, long-term occlusal surveillance, and maintenance protocols aimed at early detection of contact opening and esthetic change.

Because infraposition and proximal contact changes are expected to vary with age at implant placement, craniofacial growth status, jaw region, follow-up duration, and restorative design, quantitative synthesis in this topic should generally be framed as a random-effects problem rather than as estimation of a single common effect ref [8], ref [10]. Choice of effect measure is equally consequential: prevalence or incidence proportions, risk ratios for categorical outcomes, and mean vertical discrepancy for infraposition are not interchangeable, and their clinical interpretation should drive model specification ref [10], ref [12].

A central issue is heterogeneity. Cochran’s Q and I2 remain useful screening metrics, but both are easily overinterpreted; low power with few studies and wide uncertainty around I2 mean that apparent homogeneity often reflects imprecision rather than true consistency ref [8], ref [9]. This is especially relevant in dental implant reviews, where small observational cohorts dominate and between-study variance estimates are unstable ref [9], ref [11]. Consequently, τ2 estimation method matters: simulation work shows that commonly used DerSimonian-Laird may be suboptimal, whereas alternatives such as Paule-Mandel, restricted maximum likelihood, bootstrap-based estimators, or positive DerSimonian-Laird can perform better under different conditions ref [11].

For clinically meaningful inference, pooled confidence intervals should be complemented by prediction intervals, which express the range of effects expected in a new but exchangeable clinical setting ref [7]. This distinction is crucial when a statistically significant average effect coexists with marked dispersion across studies, as may occur for implant infraposition trajectories over long follow-up ref [7], ref [8]. Finally, assessment of small-study effects and reporting bias should be cautious: funnel-plot asymmetry and related tests are often underpowered, confounded by heterogeneity, and should not be treated as proof either for or against publication bias ref [8], ref [12].

Accordingly, evidence synthesis in this field should prioritize transparent model choice, explicit reporting of τ2/I2 uncertainty, sensitivity analyses across heterogeneity estimators, and clinically oriented interpretation of both average and predicted effects ref [7], ref [9], ref [11], ref [12].

subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Outcomes and Long-Term Tissue Stability
subsections.content:
From a clinical standpoint, infraposition and missing proximal contacts are not merely geometric changes; they are associated with tangible maintenance burdens and patient-perceived complications. In a cross-sectional evaluation of implant-supported fixed dental prostheses adjacent to natural teeth, food impaction was reported in 44.7% of embrasures, occurred more often when proximal contact loss was present, and was associated with lower overall patient satisfaction; larger embrasure surface area also increased risk, indicating that restoration contour and contact design directly influence long-term function and comfort [1]. These observations are consistent with earlier reports showing progressive loss of interproximal contact between implant restorations and adjacent teeth over time, especially on the mesial aspect, and linking this phenomenon to food impaction and the need for prosthetic maintenance.

Long-term tissue stability appears more nuanced. In the study by Jeong and Chang, food impaction itself was not significantly associated with worse plaque, bleeding, probing depth, or peri-implant bone level at recall, likely reflecting the confounding benefit of regular supportive periodontal therapy; nevertheless, several embrasure dimensions were associated with periodontal/peri-implant mucosal conditions and implant-side bone level, underscoring that tissue stability is partly prosthetically mediated rather than solely biologic [1]. In the anterior maxilla, 8-year follow-up data further showed that single implants can remain osseointegrated and esthetically acceptable while still developing relative vertical discrepancy to adjacent teeth, with minor marginal bone loss at the implant but detectable reduction of bone support at neighboring teeth in some cases [2].

Taken together, the available evidence suggests that survival of implant-supported restorations within natural dentitions should not be conflated with long-term clinical stability. Even when implants remain functionally successful, gradual changes in proximal contact, embrasure morphology, and relative crown position may compromise hygiene access, papilla support, and esthetic integration, thereby increasing the likelihood of food impaction, soft-tissue disharmony, and localized bone remodeling adjacent to the restoration [1,2]. Clinically, this supports periodic monitoring of contact tightness, embrasure form, and peri-implant as well as adjacent-tooth tissues, with a low threshold for restorative adjustment or remake when contact loss or infraposition becomes symptomatic.

Growth-related change is central to interpreting infraposition around implants placed within natural dentitions. Because osseointegrated implants behave more like ankylosed units than erupting teeth, they do not participate in the continuous dentoalveolar eruption and vertical adaptation that persist during adolescence and may continue, at lower magnitude, into adulthood ref [4]. This biologic mismatch provides a plausible mechanism for the progressive vertical discrepancy and loss of proximal contact observed over time in implant-supported restorations adjacent to natural teeth.

The adolescent literature remains especially cautionary. In a classic clinical follow-up, Thilander et al. documented infra-occlusion of implant crowns in growing patients despite successful osseointegration, and showed that dental eruption stage alone was insufficient for timing decisions; rather, residual skeletal growth was the decisive factor ref [4]. Their findings support the long-standing recommendation that implant placement in young patients should be deferred until craniofacial growth is essentially complete, with particular vigilance in the anterior maxilla where esthetic consequences of vertical discrepancy are greatest ref [4].

Importantly, growth-related risk does not end abruptly after puberty. Longitudinal cephalometric data indicate that overbite and facial height continue to change from childhood into adult life, reflecting ongoing vertical skeletal and dentoalveolar remodeling even between 25 and 45 years of age ref [14]. Such lifelong but variable vertical development helps explain why infraposition and contact loss may still emerge in adults years after apparently well-integrated implant therapy. Clinically, treatment planning should therefore consider not only chronological age, but also skeletal maturation, facial growth pattern, and the possibility of continued eruption and alveolar compensation over decades ref [4], ref [14].

The methodological strength of the evidence base on infraposition and missing proximal contact points remains constrained by the predominance of observational designs, heterogeneous outcome definitions, and inconsistent reporting of follow-up structure. In implant and prosthodontic journals more broadly, substantial risk of bias has been documented even among randomized reports, particularly for blinding, allocation concealment, and other methodological domains, underscoring the need for caution when extrapolating pooled estimates to clinical decision-making ref [15]. In this review topic, additional challenges arise from mixed age groups, varying reference landmarks for infraposition measurement, and incomplete adjustment for confounders such as residual craniofacial growth, occlusal wear, and adjacent tooth migration.

From an evidence-synthesis perspective, statistical heterogeneity is expected rather than exceptional, because effect sizes are influenced by age at implant placement, jaw region, follow-up duration, and measurement modality. Consequently, random-effects modeling is appropriate, but pooled results may still be sensitive to the estimator chosen for between-study variance. Simulation work comparing 20 estimators showed that the conventional DerSimonian-Laird approach is not uniformly optimal, whereas positive DerSimonian-Laird, bootstrap-based estimators, and in some settings Hartung-Makambi or maximum-likelihood procedures can provide more favorable performance characteristics ref [11]. More generally, interpretation should move beyond a single summary estimate toward uncertainty-aware metrics, especially when the number of studies is small and heterogeneity imprecisely estimated.

These considerations are particularly important because meta-analyses of small studies do not always reproduce the results of subsequent large trials, although agreement is often directionally acceptable ref [16]. For a clinically nuanced question such as long-term implant infraposition, pooled estimates should therefore be interpreted as average tendencies rather than fixed prognostic values. Future syntheses would benefit from preregistered protocols, standardized definitions for vertical discrepancy and contact loss, reporting of age- and sex-stratified data, and repeated-measures analyses that better reflect the time-dependent nature of these complications.

subsections.subsection_title: Technical Note on Adolescent Osseointegrated Implants
subsections.content:
Adolescent implant placement requires a different interpretive framework from adult single-implant therapy because osseointegrated fixtures behave more like ankylosed units than erupting teeth. In the classic 3-year clinical follow-up of 15 adolescents (27 implants), implant survival was excellent, yet infraocclusion developed in patients with residual craniofacial growth, particularly in the maxillary incisor region, demonstrating that chronological age alone is an unreliable guide for treatment timing ref [4].

The technical implication for this review is that infraposition around implants placed before growth completion should not be interpreted as a conventional prosthetic complication alone, but as a biologic consequence of continued dentoalveolar eruption and facial growth in the surrounding natural dentition. Thilander et al. emphasized that dental and skeletal maturation, rather than age in years, should guide case selection; body-height gain and hand-wrist maturation correlated with the magnitude of vertical discrepancy, while residual growth produced clinically relevant apical migration of the peri-implant gingival margin and relative crown shortening ref [4].

A second practical point is the regional vulnerability of the anterior maxilla. In the adolescent cohort, the largest vertical discrepancies occurred in upper incisor sites, whereas canine and premolar sites showed smaller changes, and some adjacent tooth surfaces exhibited marginal bone loss when mesiodistal space was limited ref [4]. Thus, when adolescent cases are discussed in relation to long-term missing contact points or apparent occlusal disharmony, the possibility that post-placement growth altered interproximal and vertical relationships must be explicitly considered. For contemporary evidence synthesis, adolescent implants should therefore be analyzed separately or flagged in sensitivity analyses, because their time-dependent behavior is mechanistically distinct from implants placed after skeletal maturation ref [4].
